question_text: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sharp, substernal chest pain that is worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward. He has also had nausea and myalgias. His father has coronary artery disease. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2 that is best heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

                    ### Question
                    A 23-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sharp, substernal chest pain that is worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward. He has also had nausea and myalgias. His father has coronary artery disease. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2 that is best heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Dressler syndrome
opb. Acute myocardial infarction
opc. Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection
opd. Systemic lupus erythematosus
ope. Acute viral infection

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's presentation of sharp substernal chest pain that worsens with inspiration and is relieved by leaning forward, along with the presence of a pericardial friction rub and ECG findings of diffuse ST elevations and depressed PR interval, strongly suggests acute pericarditis. Acute viral infections, particularly those caused by enteroviruses, are the most common etiology of pericarditis in young adults. While Dressler syndrome (post-myocardial infarction pericarditis) and tuberculosis can cause pericarditis, they are less likely given the acute presentation and the patient's age. The evidence paths indicating that ECG findings are associated with pericarditis support this conclusion. Therefore, the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is an acute viral infection.
